item.content:encoded:
Technical point- given the whole point of experimentation, there should be some notation on the record/s that they tested deaths on (I would expect it to be all of them, to confirm that they all share the same "new skips" property), indicating how many skips they had when acquired, and how many have been added due to Foundation tests.

I would also be entirely unsurprised if there was intentional or accidental "testing to destruction" on -4, since it was described as "almost full". How many skips is "full", and what happens when it gets full? A lot of the unanswered questions are inherently unanswerable, but this is entirely within testable range. I can also see further death tests on this being forbidden, because the Foundation doesn't really want to find out through experience what happens when a time-freezing anomalous object reaches or exceeds capacity.

Don't get me wrong, I like this one! That one part just had me wondering what kind of wedding those people were having.

item.content:encoded:
That's a good question. Right up there with, "How were the records made? How do they achieve their function? How did the first skips get onto the records to begin with?" If any of those could be answered, the Foundation would be much closer to a complete understanding of the anomaly.

It's also not as if more skips in a given play-through are necessarily beneficial. Each apparent instance of the SCP's employ could have been achieved in the course of a single freeze.

I also want to point out just how cryptic the note found with 235-4 is. There are a number of possible interpretations, and that's my favorite part about it.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I actually pointed out that very same thing while we were writing it. Technically, yes, if it simply locally froze time, then anything luminous and affected would cease to appear so to outside observers (at least while they're not moving toward the light source within the affected area), soundwaves would be frozen in place, and other weirdness would occur, but Severe preferred - and it's much easier to convey - the image of a movie freeze frame or photograph. It's mainly a stylistic choice. I think it would have been fun to explore the former case of it truly and completely arresting everything, though it's arguably weirder since the effect doesn't seem wholly consistent.

To Lonewolf, yes, 235 is necessarily immune to its own effects.

To SunRat, thank you, and you're right, and I've got no idea how I messed that up. Although, as I think about it, it might have been intentional and due to record being mislabeled. It's been so long that I can't remember. I think I'll leave it for now, as it seems like an interesting explanation, but thanks for pointing it out.

item.content:encoded: It's a matter of how you see it. Technically, the atmosphere and light within the area of effect freeze. However, any light source outside the area would illuminate just fine (much like weather). As to sound, I interpret that the effect of SCP-235 is immune to the freezing, as the record keeps playing. Those inside the area wouldn't hear anything while frozen anyway. Not sure about those "unfrozen" before the effect wears off.
